clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal dominant multisystem disorder caused by heterozygous mutations in CDC42, presenting with macrothrombocytopenia alongside developmental and structural anomalies
Haematologically it produces mild-to-moderate thrombocytopenia with large platelets
Extra-haematological features include developmental delay, distinctive facial features, lymphoedema, and structural brain, cardiac, or skeletal anomalies
Some CDC42 variants cause an autoinflammatory phenotype with recurrent fevers and macrophage activation
The specific mutation influences whether the picture is predominantly developmental, autoinflammatory, or haematological
Bleeding tendency from the macrothrombocytopenia is usually mild
It sits within the expanding group of transcription-factor and cytoskeletal-regulator inherited thrombocytopenias
Diagnosis rests on CDC42 genetic testing supported by the platelet findings and syndromic features
reference.pathophysiology: CDC42 encodes a Rho-family small GTPase that governs actin cytoskeletal dynamics, cell polarity, and intracellular signalling across many tissues. Heterozygous mutations perturb these functions, and in megakaryocytes disrupted cytoskeletal regulation impairs proplatelet formation and platelet sizing, producing macrothrombocytopenia. Because CDC42 is critical in neural, lymphatic, and skeletal development and in immune regulation, the same mutations give rise to the developmental anomalies, lymphoedema, and, for certain variants, an autoinflammatory phenotype, explaining the multisystem nature of the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Noonan syndrome and related RASopathies (for overlapping features)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film confirming macrothrombocytopenia
Neuroimaging, echocardiography, and skeletal evaluation for structural anomalies
Inflammatory markers and assessment for macrophage activation where an autoinflammatory phenotype is suspected
Platelet function testing where bleeding is disproportionate
redFlags: Features of macrophage activation syndrome or severe autoinflammation with certain CDC42 variants
Significant structural anomalies such as major cardiac or brain malformations
Bleeding disproportionate to the platelet count
Progressive neurological or growth concerns requiring multidisciplinary care
reference.prognosis: Outlook varies with the specific variant and the severity of associated anomalies; the thrombocytopenia itself is usually mild, but developmental impairment and, in autoinflammatory variants, severe inflammation can dominate the clinical course.
pitfalls: Attributing the isolated low platelet count to immune thrombocytopenia and overlooking the syndromic features
Failing to recognise the autoinflammatory phenotype in the relevant CDC42 variants
Not investigating for associated structural anomalies once the diagnosis is made
Assuming a purely haematological disorder rather than a multisystem condition
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Manage the usually mild bleeding tendency conservatively, reserving platelet transfusion for significant haemorrhage or surgical cover
Treat the autoinflammatory phenotype of specific variants with interleukin-1 or interleukin-18 directed biologic therapy
Provide developmental support with early intervention, physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy
Manage lymphoedema with skin care, compression and specialist lymphoedema therapy
Monitor for and manage structural cardiac, cerebral and skeletal anomalies with appropriate specialist follow-up
Watch for macrophage activation syndrome in autoinflammatory variants and escalate urgently with immunosuppression if it develops
Coordinate care through haematology, clinical genetics and relevant paediatric specialists
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant condition with testing of at-risk relatives
